summary:
AlbertHealth is a ground-based astronaut health-monitoring prototype designed to support crew self-check-ins and mission awareness during long-duration spaceflight. Built with Python, Streamlit, and an ESP32, it brings together manually entered sleep, fatigue, heart rate, and blood-oxygen observations; imported Earth-based Apple Watch records; and environmental measurements of air temperature, humidity, and relative light. A physical reaction-time test measures the interval between a green LED cue and a button press, then displays individual responses and the median of five valid trials.

The dashboard also uses cached NASA DONKI records to replay a linked historical solar flare and solar energetic particle event. Crew members can request a mission-information review, which activates a red LED until cleared. Health and sensor observations are saved locally, and core dashboard functions remain available without hardware.

Inspired by NASA sleep and circadian research, AlbertHealth demonstrates how multiple information sources could help users review patterns and decide when further assessment is appropriate. It is not a medical diagnostic system, a real-time radiation alarm, or validated for spaceflight.
details:
AlbertHealth is an astronaut health-monitoring prototype that combines personal health observations, environmental monitoring, cognitive-performance testing, and NASA space-weather information in one interface.

How the system works

The application was developed using Python and Streamlit, with Pandas for processing and displaying data. Astronauts can enter sleep duration, fatigue levels, heart rate, and blood oxygen through daily check-ins. The application stores these observations locally and allows users to review historical trends.

We also integrated Apple Watch health records exported through Apple Health. These Earth-based measurements demonstrate how wearable devices could contribute additional health information to a future system.

Hardware integration

Our team developed an ESP32-based device using Arduino C++. It incorporates a DHT11 temperature and humidity sensor, a photoresistor for relative ambient-light measurements, two LEDs, and a physical button.

The ESP32 communicates with AlbertHealth through USB serial communication at 115200 baud. Sensor readings and reaction-time results are transmitted as JSON messages.

Our physical reaction-time test activates a green LED after a randomized delay. When the participant presses the button, the ESP32 measures the response in milliseconds. AlbertHealth records five valid trials and calculates their median. During testing, we successfully completed a five-trial session with a median response time of 317 milliseconds.

NASA data and mission awareness

AlbertHealth incorporates authentic historical NASA DONKI records, including a linked solar flare and solar energetic particle event from May 11, 2024. Users can request a mission-information review, activating the ESP32's red LED until the notification is cleared.

These historical records provide mission context. The system does not measure individual radiation exposure or issue real-time radiation warnings.

Benefits and future development

AlbertHealth brings multiple information sources into one interface, helping users review sleep, fatigue, cognitive responses, and environmental conditions together.

The system is designed to retain core software functions when the ESP32 is disconnected, and NASA records are cached for offline demonstrations.

Our prototype is not a validated medical device. Future improvements could include continuous monitoring, secure multi-crew data storage, and research-based analysis of long-term health and environmental trends.

Our goal is to demonstrate how integrated monitoring and accessible information could support crew awareness and inform future astronaut health-monitoring systems.
